issues.legal_issue: An eyewitness’s testimony may remain reliable despite discrepancies attributed to an earlier dishonest investigation when the discrepancies do not show deliberate fabrication or eliminate the opportunity to observe the crime.
material_facts: The eyewitness was present with the victim on the platform and testified that he saw the attack from nearby while having his shoes polished.
His earlier recorded accounts differed on some details, including the number of assailants and shots, and omitted some details of the final shot.
The court found the earlier investigation dishonest and found the discrepancies insufficient to establish that the eyewitness had deliberately improved his account.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness’s testimony was credible, and the trial court was wrong to reject it on the basis of the cited discrepancies and the asserted lack of opportunity to observe.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the eyewitness’s evidence in light of the circumstances of observation and the nature of the discrepancies. It held that discrepancies arising from an earlier investigation found not to be honest could not be given the significance the trial court assigned them, and that the suddenness of the incident alone did not establish that the witness lacked a sufficient opportunity to see the assailants.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and eyewitness_present_near_victim and eyewitness_had_opportunity_to_observe and discrepancies_do_not_show_deliberate_fabrication

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.eyewitness_present_near_victim: An eyewitness was present close to the victim when the attack occurred.
predicates.eyewitness_had_opportunity_to_observe: The eyewitness had an opportunity to observe the assailants and the attack.
predicates.discrepancies_do_not_show_deliberate_fab: The differences between the eyewitness’s accounts did not establish that the witness deliberately fabricated or improved the account.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, nearby presence and a sufficient opportunity to observe can support acceptance of eyewitness testimony if discrepancies do not show deliberate fabrication.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a test identification parade reduces the evidentiary value of an identification made in court, but does not make that identification insufficient when it is corroborated by other evidence.
material_facts: One eyewitness identified several accused in court about three years after the incident, and no test identification parade had been held.
The court found that this identification was corroborated by another eyewitness and by confessions it held admissible, voluntary and believable.
issues.conclusion: The in-court identification was not sufficient by itself, but its corroboration made it sufficient to support the relevant findings.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principle in the identification case cited as Kanan (AIR 1980 SC 1382): absence of a test identification parade diminishes the evidentiary value of in-court identification. It nevertheless held that corroboration by another eyewitness and by admissible, voluntary and believable confessions could make the identification sufficient.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.in_court_identification_without_test_par: A witness identified an accused in court without an earlier test identification parade.
predicates.identification_corroborated_by_independe: Other evidence corroborated the witness’s identification.

issues.definition: An in-court identification made without a test parade may be sufficient when independent evidence corroborates it.

issues.legal_issue: A prior investigation may be found dishonest, while a later reinvestigation may be found free of an oblique motive, where the record supports those distinct conclusions.
material_facts: The initial report was recorded and reached the police station later than the recorded timings suggested, and it reached the magistrate after a delay.

The initial investigators sought to connect a revolver to the shooting despite the recovery of spent cartridges indicating use of a pistol, made a false statement in a remand application about recovering the weapon, and made no serious effort to secure the accused’s attendance at trial.
The victim’s family testified that police officers pressured and threatened them not to name gang members.

A senior railway police officer had grounds to doubt the initial investigation; the later investigator obtained further information and material before seeking permission to reinvestigate and invoke the special statute.
The court found no material showing that the senior officer or the later investigator acted to help the victim’s family or to frustrate bail applications.
issues.conclusion: The initial investigation was not honest, and the subsequent reinvestigation was not conducted with an oblique motive.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the investigators’ conduct against the evidence as a whole, including the timing and handling of the report and physical evidence, the treatment of witnesses, and the material gathered before reinvestigation. It held that the later investigator could seek permission to reinvestigate and invoke the special statute on the basis of material collected during the inquiry; the absence of a specific allegation of dishonesty in the initial complaint did not establish improper motive.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.initial_investigation_contains_material_: The initial investigators handled the report or physical evidence irregularly, pressured witnesses, or failed to take reasonable steps to advance the prosecution.
predicates.later_investigation_supported_by_gathere: The later investigator gathered material supporting further investigation before seeking permission or taking consequential investigative steps.
predicates.no_evidence_of_improper_motive: The record did not establish that the later investigation was undertaken for an improper purpose.

issues.definition: In an appeal from acquittal, material irregularities in an initial investigation and a later investigation supported by gathered material, without evidence of improper motive, can support finding the first dishonest and the second unmotivated.

issues.legal_issue: A confession recorded in two parts can comply with the required warning and voluntariness inquiry when those safeguards are given before the confession begins and the parts form one continuous statement.
material_facts: Before the accused gave their confessional statements, the recording officer warned them that they were not bound to confess and that a confession could be used against them.
The officer questioned each accused about willingness to confess and whether the confession was being made under pressure, and allowed time for reconsideration before recording the statement.
The statements were recorded in two parts, and the officer again checked willingness when the accused returned to make the statement.
issues.conclusion: Recording the confessions in two parts did not breach Rule 15(2) of the applicable rules because the warning and voluntariness inquiry preceded the confession as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the TADA Act and Rule 15(2) of the TADA Rules require the recording officer to explain that the person is not bound to confess and that a confession may be used in evidence, and to question the person to ascertain voluntariness before recording it. The court held that the two parts could be treated as one continuous confession and that the warning and inquiry need not be repeated at the start of the second part. It rejected the contention that the separate requirements of Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applied to a confession recorded under Section 15.

predicates.confession_recorded_under_special_statut: The confession was recorded under a statutory power permitting a police officer to record confessions.
predicates.warning_given_before_confession: Before the confession was recorded, the officer explained that the person need not confess and that a confession could be used in evidence.
predicates.voluntariness_ascertained_before_confess: Before recording the confession, the officer questioned the person to ascertain that it was being made voluntarily.
predicates.separate_parts_form_continuous_statement: The separate recorded parts constituted one continuous confession rather than independent statements.

issues.definition: A confession recorded in separate continuous parts is not invalid merely because the safeguards were given and checked before the confession began rather than repeated for each part.

issues.legal_issue: Substantial compliance with the required certificate and memorandum can satisfy the recording safeguards even when their wording or arrangement does not reproduce the prescribed form exactly.
material_facts: The recording officer’s certificates and memorandums did not use the prescribed form and wording and combined matters that the rules described separately.
The records stated that the officer had ascertained voluntariness, recorded the statements, read them over, and confirmed that the accused accepted them as accurate.
The statutory warning appeared in the body of the recorded statements rather than in the memorandum at the end.
issues.conclusion: The confessions were not inadmissible merely because the certificates and memorandums departed from the prescribed form and wording; the trial court erred in treating that departure as noncompliance.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 15(3) of the TADA Rules requires a contemporaneous certificate and memorandum to establish that the safeguards were followed and the confession was recorded accurately. The court held that the required matters are mandatory, but that the precise form and words are not, if the requirements have been substantially complied with. It distinguished the mandatory substance of the safeguard from its presentation and arrangement.

predicates.confession_recorded_under_special_statut: The confession was recorded under a statutory power permitting a police officer to record confessions.
predicates.contemporaneous_record_shows_required_sa: The contemporaneous record showed that the officer addressed voluntariness, the warning, and the accuracy and reading over of the confession.
predicates.wording_or_arrangement_differs_from_pres: The certificate or memorandum differed from the prescribed wording or arrangement.

issues.definition: A departure from the prescribed wording or arrangement alone does not invalidate a confession when a contemporaneous record substantially demonstrates the required safeguards.

issues.legal_issue: A confession recorded under the special statutory procedure is substantive evidence against its maker and may be used against a co-accused if it is admissible, voluntary and believable.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on confessions recorded under the special statutory procedure.
The court found that the confessions were voluntarily made, reliable, and corroborated on material points by eyewitness evidence and other testimony.
Some confessions admitted the makers’ participation in the killing and in the activities of the gangs.
issues.conclusion: The confessions could be relied on as substantive evidence against their makers and could also be used against co-accused, subject to their being admissible, voluntary and believable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the TADA Act makes qualifying confessions to police officers admissible and is an important departure from ordinary law. The court relied on Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, (1994) 3 SCC 569, for the provision’s purpose and constitutionality, and on State through Superintendent of Police, CBI/SIT v. Nalini for the proposition that such a confession is substantive evidence against its maker and may be used against a co-accused when admissible, voluntary and believable. It also considered the differing views in Nalini on the degree of corroboration and discussed Kalpnath Rai v. State, (1997) 8 SCC 732.

rule.if: confession_recorded_under_special_statutory_power and confession_is_admissible and confession_is_voluntary and confession_is_believable

predicates.confession_recorded_under_special_statut: The confession was recorded under a statutory power permitting a police officer to record confessions.
predicates.confession_is_admissible: The confession satisfies the applicable admissibility requirements.
predicates.confession_is_believable: The court finds the confession believable.

issues.definition: A confession recorded under special statutory authority may be used against its maker and a co-accused when it is admissible, voluntary and believable.

issues.legal_issue: A co-accused’s confession that creates strong suspicion against an accused police officer is not, without independent evidence, a safe basis for conviction.
material_facts: The police officers were charged with conspiring to conceal evidence and screen the actual offenders through a dishonest investigation.
The only evidence implicating those officers was the confessional statements of co-accused.
The confessions created strong suspicion about the officers’ connections with the gangs and possible assistance, but there was no independent evidence of their alleged participation.
issues.conclusion: The court did not consider it safe to convict the police officers solely on the co-accused confessions and affirmed their acquittals.
issues.legal_principle: Although a confession under Section 15 of the TADA Act may be substantive evidence against a co-accused if admissible, voluntary and believable, the court held that the evidence in this case did not safely support conviction of the police officers without independent evidence. Its discussion of Section 30 of the Evidence Act and the views in Nalini recognized the need for caution in relying on a confession against another accused.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.accused_is_charged_with_conspiracy: The accused was charged with participating in a conspiracy.
predicates.only_evidence_against_accused_is_coaccus: The only evidence implicating the accused consisted of confessions made by co-accused.
predicates.confession_creates_suspicion_without_ind: The confessions raised suspicion but lacked independent evidentiary support for the accused’s alleged participation.

issues.definition: In an appeal from acquittal, a co-accused confession that raises suspicion but lacks independent support does not safely sustain a conspiracy conviction by itself.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence of violent or illegal gang activity, together with credible confessions describing the gangs’ terror and terrorist acts, may support a finding that the accused participated in terrorist acts.
material_facts: The confessions of the accused described gang activities, the creation of terror, and the killing as part of the gangs’ activities.
Witnesses gave evidence about threats, assaults, and other illegal activities, although some testimony was general or did not independently describe a specific terrorist act.
The court found that the witness evidence corroborated the confessions on material points and held the relevant accused guilty of terrorist acts.
issues.conclusion: The court held the relevant accused guilty of offences under Section 3(3) of the TADA Act.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Section 3 of the TADA Act to the evidence as a whole. It accepted that some witnesses’ evidence, standing alone, was not sufficiently specific to prove terrorist acts, but treated it as corroboration of the confessional admissions describing the gangs’ terror and activities.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.confession_describes_terrorist_gang_acti: A confession described the accused’s participation in gang activity involving terror or terrorist acts.
predicates.witness_evidence_corroborates_material_p: Witness testimony about threats, violence, or related illegal activity corroborated material parts of the confession.

issues.definition: In an appeal from acquittal, a confession describing terrorist gang activity, corroborated on material points by witness evidence, may support a finding of participation in terrorist acts.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed discovery of a weapon is not established as a discovery under the discovery rule when the supporting witnesses do not support the prosecution account and the record does not reliably prove the discovery.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on an alleged discovery of a pistol by an accused as corroboration.
The panch witnesses did not support the prosecution’s account of the discovery.
The court found it difficult to hold that the event was a discovery within Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act.
issues.conclusion: The court did not rely on the alleged discovery as a circumstance corroborating the eyewitness evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act and held, on the evidence concerning the alleged recovery, that it could not be treated as a discovery contemplated by that provision.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and prosecution_relies_on_discovery and discovery_witnesses_do_not_support_account and discovery_not_reliably_proved

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.prosecution_relies_on_discovery: The prosecution relies on an accused’s alleged discovery of an object as evidence.
predicates.discovery_witnesses_do_not_support_accou: The witnesses called to support the discovery do not support the prosecution’s account.
predicates.discovery_not_reliably_proved: The evidence does not reliably establish that the claimed discovery occurred as alleged.
